item.title: Bay Street’s Carbon Footprint Rivals Nations: New Report
item.dc:creator: rayan
item.content:encoded: Eighteen Toronto banks, pensions and asset managers responsible for financing emissions that are almost 2x Canada’s total emissions, nearly 100x City of Toronto’s emissions.

wp:postmeta.wp:meta_value: Header for the Bay Street Climate Report , with the text: A report by the Toronto Climate Observatory, a research hub based at the University of Toronto, found that Toronto’s Financial Institutions were responsible for 1.44 billion tCO2e in 2022.That is almost 100x the City of Toronto’s emissions, and almost 2x Canada’s national emissions. While these numbers are astounding, they are also minimums. Read more about the report and its key recommendation at http://climateobservatory.ca/baystreetclimatemonitor.

Header for the Bay Street Climate Report , with the text: A report by the Toronto Climate Observatory, a research hub based at the University of Toronto, found that Toronto’s Financial Institutions were responsible for 1.44 billion tCO2e in 2022.That is almost 100x the City of Toronto’s emissions, and almost 2x Canada’s national emissions. JUST CLIMATE FUTURES

         Grounded Research. Interdisciplinary Insights. Local Action.

The Toronto Climate Observatory is a research and knowledge hub dedicated to supporting

just, place-based climate action across the Greater Toronto Area. We combine

interdisciplinary expertise, community partnerships, local voices, and open

data to inform planning, resilience, and equity in a changing climate.

Our mission? Advancing collaborative, equitable

climate action rooted in justice and place.


Learn more

{"name":"hop-content","children":[{"name":"hop-section","props":{"anchor":false,"name":"Climate Data Practices","attrs":{"id":"climate-data-practices"}},"children":[{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"33.33","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"14-c4","parentId":"14-c3","partialId":14,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c4","index":0,"id":"14-c5","partialId":14,"styleRef":1091,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/cropped-pexels-christina-morillo-1181271-scaled-1.jpg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1235,"size":""}}],"styleRef":1090,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"66.67","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"14-c6","parentId":"14-c3","partialId":14,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c6","index":0,"id":"14-c7","partialId":14,"styleRef":1093,"type":"content","props":{"content":"CLIMATE DATA PRACTICES IN THE
GREATER TORONTO AREA"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c6","index":0,"id":"14-c8","partialId":14,"styleRef":1094,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

This collaborative and multidisciplinary research project draws on practice theory as a tool for critically interrogating the role of data and information in in shaping how we know what we know about the ways in which climate change is impacting the Greater Toronto Area in the present, along with predictions for how this will accelerate in the future. We draw on a variety of methods including ethnographic fieldwork, interview studies, and document analysis to understand the role of data in the daily work and climate imaginaries of a range of publics, user groups, and communities across the region including youth climate activists, emergency managers, artists, transit planners, urban agriculture practitioners, and municipal governments. Thus project contributes climate data practices as a methodological approach that is suitable for helping to gain analytic purchase on these questions across a broad range of contexts. This is necessary to understand the contemporary knowledge politics of climate change, and to guide the creation of alternative information infrastructures that support place-based, plural, and just climate action.<\/p>"}}],"styleRef":1092,"type":"content"}],"id":"14-c3","parentId":"14-c2","partialId":14,"styleRef":1089,"type":"content"}],"id":"14-c2","parentId":"14-c1","partialId":14,"styleRef":1088,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-section","props":{"anchor":false,"name":"Equity in Disaster Modelling","attrs":{"id":"equity-in-disaster-modelling"}},"children":[{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"33.33","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"14-c11","parentId":"14-c10","partialId":14,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c11","index":0,"id":"14-c12","partialId":14,"styleRef":1081,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c25","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/equity_disaster_modelling-scaled.jpg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1212,"size":""}}],"styleRef":1080,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"66.67","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"14-c13","parentId":"14-c10","partialId":14,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c13","index":0,"id":"14-c14","partialId":14,"styleRef":1083,"type":"content","props":{"content":"EQUITY IN CLIMATE AND DISASTER RISK MODELING"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c13","index":0,"id":"14-c15","partialId":14,"styleRef":1084,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

Societal efforts to understand and mitigate threats posed by hazards such as earthquakes, floods, and climate change are informed by complex spatial risk models produced by experts from physical sciences and engineering. Despite decades of research that demonstrated the disproportionate effects of disasters on vulnerable groups, current approaches to risk modeling lack robust methods for taking such equity concerns into account. Differential disaster burden has been observed along wider axes of societal marginalization, including income and social status, age, race, gender, and disability. Increasingly, scholars are calling attention to the need for disaster and climate risk models to account for equity to better integrate these concerns into practice. This project brings together expertise in disaster and climate risk modeling, critical theory, and science and technology studies to achieve three objectives evaluate the extent to which equity and justice concerns are incorporated into current disaster and climate risk models, estimate the character and order-of-magnitude size of potential disaster and climate impacts that are being missed or mischaracterized through failure to account for equity issues in these models, and generate recommendations on how quantitative risk models for the region can incorporate equity in the future.<\/p>


<\/p>"}}],"styleRef":1082,"type":"content"}],"id":"14-c10","parentId":"14-c9","partialId":14,"styleRef":1079,"type":"content"}],"id":"14-c9","parentId":"14-c1","partialId":14,"styleRef":1078,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c15"},{"name":"hop-section","props":{"anchor":false,"name":"Weather Risk Communication","attrs":{"id":"weather-risk-communication"}},"children":[{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"33.33","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"14-c18","parentId":"14-c17","partialId":14,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c18","index":0,"id":"14-c19","partialId":14,"styleRef":1101,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/cropped-image.jpg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1223,"size":""}}],"styleRef":1100,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"66.67","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"14-c20","parentId":"14-c17","partialId":14,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c20","index":0,"id":"14-c21","partialId":14,"styleRef":1103,"type":"content","props":{"content":"COMMUNICATING SEVERE WEATHER RISK"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c20","index":0,"id":"14-c22","partialId":14,"styleRef":1104,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

In Ontario, severe weather events are becoming increasingly frequent and intense, causing damage and disruptions in the places where they occur. People with visual impairments face significant barriers to receiving timely and instructive communications about risk and safety during severe weather events. Such information is necessary for \u201cprotective decision-making\u201d - decisions that individuals and communities make in advance of and during disasters that impact their safety with regards to these events. Currently, authoritative weather risk communication in Ontario does not meet the needs of people with visual impairments. This two-year research project seeks to address the accessibility gaps that exist within the current disaster response measures and communication channels through design research into the needs, capacities, and constraints of people with visual disabilities in Ontario. Drawing on research design methods and inclusive design, the goal of this project is to develops a better understanding of these issues, and design and test communication strategies and technologies to alleviate them.<\/p>"}}],"styleRef":1102,"type":"content"}],"id":"14-c17","parentId":"14-c16","partialId":14,"styleRef":1099,"type":"content"}],"id":"14-c16","parentId":"14-c1","partialId":14,"styleRef":1098,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-section","props":{"anchor":false,"name":"TCO Summer School","attrs":{"id":"tco-summer-school"}},"children":[{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"33.33","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"14-c25","parentId":"14-c24","partialId":14,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c25","index":0,"id":"14-c26","partialId":14,"styleRef":1108,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/cropped-Summer-School.jpg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1237,"size":""}}],"styleRef":1107,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"66.67","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"14-c27","parentId":"14-c24","partialId":14,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c27","index":0,"id":"14-c28","partialId":14,"styleRef":1110,"type":"content","props":{"content":"THE TORONTO CLIMATE SUMMER SCHOOL"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c27","index":0,"id":"14-c29","partialId":14,"styleRef":1111,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

The goal of this project is to develop and pilot curricular infrastructure for a six week full credit undergraduate course at the School of the Environment - University of Toronto. This is to fulfill a timely and unmet need for intensive pedagogy that foregrounds interdisciplinarity, applied impact, and climate justice. Combining elements of field courses, experiential learning, and research-based summer camps, this summer course will offer students training in research skills, experience with interdisciplinary research projects, and exposure to a wide array of research, policy, and practice domains drawn from the physical sciences, social sciences and humanities. The curriculum will include daily lectures, skill-based workshops, field visits, brown-bag lunches from UofT experts and community partners, and curated e-modules. In addition, each student will complete an independent research project advised by one of the TCO faculty.<\/p>"}}],"styleRef":1109,"type":"content"}],"id":"14-c24","parentId":"14-c23","partialId":14,"styleRef":1106,"type":"content"}],"id":"14-c23","parentId":"14-c1","partialId":14,"styleRef":1105,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-section","props":{"anchor":false,"name":"Reusable Sections","attrs":{"id":"reusable-sections"}},"children":[{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"33.33","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"14-c32","parentId":"14-c31","partialId":14,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c32","index":0,"id":"14-c33","partialId":14,"styleRef":1115,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/retrofits-scaled.jpg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1252,"size":""}}],"styleRef":1114,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"66.67","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"14-c34","parentId":"14-c31","partialId":14,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c34","index":0,"id":"14-c35","partialId":14,"styleRef":1117,"type":"content","props":{"content":"EXPLORING MORE JUST ENGAGEMENTS WITH ENERGY MODELING FOR BUILDING RETROFITS"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"14-c34","index":0,"id":"14-c36","partialId":14,"styleRef":1118,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

According to the Canada Energy Regulator (CER), buildings account for 26% of the country\u2019s overall energy consumption, with other sources citing 40% as a more realistic number. Existing buildings will be inadvertently impacted by climate change in multifarious ways, and retrofitting requires long-term energy performance simulations that consider the future effects of climate change. While powerful, computational approaches to energy transition ignore the differential impacts of transition policies, including the need to consider trade-offs between what is just or good from an occupant perspective, and what is optimal from an energy transition lens. This project will investigate how a modeling-based approach to energy transitions can support more equitable participation and just decision making for building retrofits.<\/p>"}}],"styleRef":1116,"type":"content"}],"id":"14-c31","parentId":"14-c30","partialId":14,"styleRef":1113,"type":"content"}],"id":"14-c30","parentId":"14-c1","partialId":14,"styleRef":1112,"type":"content"}],"id":"14-c1","partialId":14,"styleRef":334,"type":"content"}

Dr. Robert Soden is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science & School of the Environment at the University of Toronto and the founder of TCO. He works in the areas of crisis informatics, human-centered computing (HCC), and science and technology studies (STS). His research uses a range of ethnographic, participatory, and design research methods to evaluate and improve the technologies we use to understand and respond to disasters and climate change. Dr. Soden has 20 years of academic and industry experience developing human-centered approaches to environmental modelling, including work with organizations such as the World Bank, the United Nations, and the World Resources Institute.<\/p>"}},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c9","index":2,"id":"9-c12","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c13","parentId":"9-c12","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"http:\/\/robertsoden.io\/"}},"domuuid":"9-c10"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c6","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c15","parentId":"9-c14","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c15","index":0,"id":"9-c16","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2022\/11\/cropped-Steve-Easterbrook.jpg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":519,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c413"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c17","parentId":"9-c14","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c17","index":0,"id":"9-c18","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Steve Easterbrook

Dr Steve Easterbrook is a Professor in the Department of Computer Science and the Director of the School of the Environment at the University of Toronto. He studies the development of computational models for understanding climate change, along with the role of models and data visualizations for sharing knowledge about climate and sustainability with other communities.<\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c17","index":2,"id":"9-c20","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c21","parentId":"9-c20","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"http:\/\/www.cs.toronto.edu\/~sme\/"}},"domuuid":"9-c32"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c14","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c23","parentId":"9-c22","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c23","index":0,"id":"9-c24","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/SS2.png","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1074,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c405"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c25","parentId":"9-c22","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c25","index":0,"id":"9-c26","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Samar Sabie

Dr. Samar Sabie is an incoming Assistant Professor at the Institute for Culture, Communication, and Information Technology (ICCIT) with a graduate appointment at the Daniels Faculty of Architecture, and Landscape, and Design at the University of Toronto. Her  research examines how design as a socio-material practice supports communities in reconfiguring or reimagining the environments they inhabit in more equitable ways despite cultural, generational, and political differences. Her approach is highly interdisciplinary, combining design and making with ethnography, critical theory, and pedagogy development in community-based contexts.<\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c25","index":2,"id":"9-c28","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c29","parentId":"9-c28","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"https:\/\/samarsabie.com"}},"domuuid":"9-c23"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c22","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c31","parentId":"9-c30","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c31","index":0,"id":"9-c32","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/IA.png","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1029,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c413"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c33","parentId":"9-c30","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c33","index":0,"id":"9-c34","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Ishtiaque Ahmed
"},"domuuid":"9-c415"},{"name":"hop-text","parentId":"9-c33","index":0,"id":"9-c35","partialId":9,"styleRef":1219,"type":"content","slot":null,"props":{"content":"

Dr. Ishtiaque Ahmad is an Assistant Professor of Computer Science at the University of Toronto. He directs the Third Space research group at the DGP Lab. He is also a graduate faculty member of the School of Environment, a Faculty Fellow at the Schwartz Reisman Institute for Technology and Society, and a Senior Fellow at the Massey College. He co-organizes the monthly UofT Critical Computing Seminar that hosts speakers analyzing computer science and its applications from the perspectives of marginalization, bias, and oppression. His research interest is situated at the intersection of computer science and the critical social sciences. His work is often motivated by social justice and sustainability issues, and he puts them in the academic contexts of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and Information and Communication Technology and Development (ICTD). He operates through a wide range of technical and methodological apparatuses from ethnography to design, and from NLP to tangible user interface. <\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c33","index":2,"id":"9-c36","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c37","parentId":"9-c36","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"https:\/\/www.ishtiaque.net\/"}},"domuuid":"9-c40"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c30","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c39","parentId":"9-c38","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c39","index":0,"id":"9-c40","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/KC.png","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1039,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c227"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c41","parentId":"9-c38","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c41","index":0,"id":"9-c42","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Karen Chapple
"},"domuuid":"9-c229"},{"name":"hop-text","parentId":"9-c41","index":0,"id":"9-c43","partialId":9,"styleRef":1219,"type":"content","slot":null,"props":{"content":"

Dr. Karen Chapple is the Director of the School of Cities at the University of Toronto, where she also serves as Professor in the Department of Geography and Planning. She is Professor Emerita of City & Regional Planning at the University of California, Berkeley, where she served as department chair and held the Carmel P. Friesen Chair in Urban Studies. Chapple studies inequalities in the planning, development, and governance of regions in the Americas, with a focus on economic development and housing. Her recent books include Planning Sustainable Cities and Regions: Towards More Equitable Development (Routledge, 2015), which won the John Friedmann Book Award from the American Collegiate Schools of Planning; Transit-Oriented Displacement or Community Dividends? Understanding the Effects of Smarter Growth on Communities (with Anastasia Loukaitou-Sideris, MIT Press, 2019); and Fragile Governance and Local Economic Development: Theory and Evidence from Peripheral Regions in Latin America (with Sergio Montero, Routledge, 2018). <\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c41","index":2,"id":"9-c44","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c45","parentId":"9-c44","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"http:\/\/karenchapple.com\/"}},"domuuid":"9-c48"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c38","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c47","parentId":"9-c46","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c47","index":0,"id":"9-c48","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/MC.png","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1041,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c235"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c49","parentId":"9-c46","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c49","index":0,"id":"9-c50","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Michael Classens

Dr. Michael Classens is an Assistant Professor in the School of the Environment at the University of Toronto. Prior to joining the School, Classens taught in Trent University\u2019s Sustainable Agriculture and Food Systems program for the past three years. His research is focused broadly on questions of social and environmental sustainability, with a particular focus on how these dynamics are frustrated by, and enabled through, food systems. His teaching, research and advocacy work are broadly motivated by commitments to social and environmental justice, particularly within the context of the food system.<\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c49","index":2,"id":"9-c52","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c53","parentId":"9-c52","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"https:\/\/www.foodandchange.com\/"}},"domuuid":"9-c56"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c46","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c55","parentId":"9-c54","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c55","index":0,"id":"9-c56","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/FC.png","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1027,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c243"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c57","parentId":"9-c54","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c57","index":0,"id":"9-c58","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Fanny Chevalier

Dr. Fanny Chevalier is an Assistant Professor in Computer Science and Statistics. Her research lies at the intersection of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) and Information Visualization (Infovis). She is interested in addressing the challenges involved in the design, implementation, and evaluation of novel interactive tools supporting visual analytics and creative activities, with primary focus on interactive visualization for the visual exploration of rich and complex data, visualization education and statistical communication, and computing tools supporting the flow of creativity.<\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c57","index":2,"id":"9-c60","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c61","parentId":"9-c60","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"http:\/\/fannychevalier.net\/"}},"domuuid":"9-c64"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c54","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c241"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c63","parentId":"9-c62","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c63","index":0,"id":"9-c64","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/TM.png","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1047,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c243"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c65","parentId":"9-c62","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c65","index":0,"id":"9-c66","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Tegan Maharaj

Dr. Tegan Maharaj is an Assistant Professor in the Faculty of Information, and an affiliate of the Vector Institute and Schwartz-Reisman Institute for Technology and Society. She is also a managing editor at the\u202fJournal of Machine Learning Research (JMLR),\u202fthe top scholarly journal in machine learning, and co-founder of\u202fClimate Change AI (CCAI), an organization which catalyzes impactful work applying machine learning to problems of climate change.\u202fPrior to joining the iSchool, Tegan did her PhD at Mila and Polytechnique Montreal, where she was an NSERC and IVADO awarded scholar with\u202fChristopher Pal. Tegan is broadly interested in studying \u201cwhat goes into\u201d AI systems \u2013 not only data, but the broader learning environment including task design and specification, loss function, and regularization; as well as the broader societal context of deployment including privacy considerations, trends and incentives, norms, and human biases. She is concerned and passionate about AI ethics, safety, and the application of ML to environmental management, health, and social welfare.<\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c65","index":2,"id":"9-c68","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c69","parentId":"9-c68","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"http:\/\/www.teganmaharaj.com\/"}},"domuuid":"9-c72"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c62","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c71","parentId":"9-c70","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c71","index":0,"id":"9-c72","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2022\/11\/cropped-zuSlU2l_400x400.jpg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":767,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c243"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c73","parentId":"9-c70","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c73","index":0,"id":"9-c74","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Fadi Masoud

Fadi Masoud is an Assistant Professor of Landscape Architecture and Urbanism and the Director of the Centre for Landscape Research. Prior to joining the University of Toronto, Masoud held teaching and research appointments at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Department of Urban Studies and Planning and was an affiliated research faculty with the MIT Leventhal Center for Advanced Urbanism. Masoud holds a Bachelors of Environmental Studies from the University of Waterloo's School of Planning, specializing in Urban Design and Urban Development, a Masters of Landscape Architecture from the University of Toronto, and a Post-Professional Master in Landscape Architecture from Harvard University's Graduate School of Design, where he graduated with distinction. Masoud's research and design work engages the landscape as an operational force in shaping urbanism. His work aims to establish relationships between large-scale dynamic environmental systems, social equity and vulnerability, design, and the instrumentality of planning frameworks, policies, and codes.<\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c73","index":2,"id":"9-c76","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c77","parentId":"9-c76","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"https:\/\/www.daniels.utoronto.ca\/people\/core-faculty\/fadi-masoud"}},"domuuid":"9-c80"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c70","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c79","parentId":"9-c78","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c79","index":0,"id":"9-c80","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2022\/11\/Hanna-Morris.jpg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":532,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c243"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c81","parentId":"9-c78","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c81","index":0,"id":"9-c82","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Hanna Morris

Dr. Hanna Morris is an Assistant Professor at the School of the Environment at the University of Toronto with research interests in climate change media and communication, culture and politics, and transnational climate movements. Previously, Hanna was a Postdoctoral Fellow at the Annenberg School for Communication at the University of Pennsylvania. Currently, she is writing a book entitled Apocalyptic Authoritarianism: Climate Crisis, Media, and Power. Hanna\u2019s research and writing have been published in various academic journals and popular media outlets including Environmental Communication, Media Theory, Politique Am\u00e9ricaine, Reading The Pictures, and Earth Island Journal. She also co-edited the book entitled Climate Change and Journalism: Negotiating Rifts of Time. Her scholarship has been recognized by the IAMCR Stuart Hall Award, New Directions for Climate Communication Research Fellowship, and Top Paper Awards from the International Communication Association and Association for Environmental Studies and Sciences. <\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c81","index":2,"id":"9-c84","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c85","parentId":"9-c84","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"https:\/\/hannamorris.com\/"}},"domuuid":"9-c88"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c78","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c87","parentId":"9-c86","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c87","index":0,"id":"9-c88","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/JR.png","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1038,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c291"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c89","parentId":"9-c86","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c89","index":0,"id":"9-c90","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"John Robinson

Dr. John Robinson is a U of T Professor in the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy and the School of the Environment, Presidential Advisor on the Environment, Climate Change and Sustainability and has established the Urban Climate Action Project (UCAP) to work with the City of Toronto in support of climate action. Dr. Robinson\u2019s research focuses on the intersection of climate change mitigation, adaptation and sustainability, the use of visualization, modeling, and citizen engagement to explore sustainable futures, sustainable buildings and urban design, and the intersection of sustainability, social and technological change, behavior change, and community engagement processes. <\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c89","index":2,"id":"9-c92","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c93","parentId":"9-c92","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"http:\/\/johnbrobinson.info\/"}},"domuuid":"9-c104"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c86","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c95","parentId":"9-c94","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c95","index":0,"id":"9-c96","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/IR.png","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1030,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c299"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c97","parentId":"9-c94","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c97","index":0,"id":"9-c98","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Imara Rolston

Dr. Imara Rolston is an Assistant Professor in the Dalla Lana School of Public Health. He is currently engaged in translating learning and insights from years of AIDS intervention into the creation of new frontiers for community-led climate resilience across Toronto\u2019s Neighborhood Improvement Areas (NIAs). As a member of the City of Toronto\u2019s ResilientTO team he developed a citywide Resilient Conversations civic-engagement initiative that worked with grassroots local leaders to convene resilience conversations across seven of the city\u2019s NIAs. He also led the development of the strategy\u2019s equity-focused Neighbourhood Resilience Action that will prioritize resilience-building in NIAs across the city. Dr. Rolston holds a B.A from the University of Toronto in Political Science and Sustainable Development and a M.A in Adult Education and Community Development from the Ontario Institute for Studies in Education (OISE) at U of T. He earned his doctorate in Social Psychology from the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE). <\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c97","index":2,"id":"9-c100","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c101","parentId":"9-c100","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"https:\/\/www.communityclimateresiliencelab.org\/team-memebrs\/imara-ajani-rolston"}},"domuuid":"9-c112"}],"domuuid":"9-c9"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c94","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c103","parentId":"9-c102","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c103","index":0,"id":"9-c104","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/NSS.png","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1044,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c307"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c105","parentId":"9-c102","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c105","index":0,"id":"9-c106","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Nicole Spiegelaar

Dr. Nicole Spiegelaar is an Assistant Professor at Trinity College and the School of the Environment. She works with complex adaptive systems theory and interdisciplinary knowledge integration to address sustainability challenges. Her past research involved subarctic agroecology, food sovereignty and food security in Indigenous communities and her more recent work explores mental wellness implications of traditional harvests and food system transition among these communities. Nicole is the Associate Director of the Trinity Sustainability Initiative which connects the classroom, student research, internships, and campus sustainability through experiential learning; her work in the group focuses on socio-ecological relations in the process of decolonizing and naturalizing our food systems. <\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c105","index":2,"id":"9-c108","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c109","parentId":"9-c108","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"https:\/\/www.environment.utoronto.ca\/node\/285"}},"domuuid":"9-c120"}],"domuuid":"9-c311"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c102","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c111","parentId":"9-c110","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c111","index":0,"id":"9-c112","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/NS.png","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1043,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c315"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c113","parentId":"9-c110","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c113","index":0,"id":"9-c114","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Nidhi Subramanyam

Dr. Nidhi Subramanyam is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Geography and Planning. Her ongoing research investigates just approaches to plan and govern water and wastewater infrastructures in the face of rapid urbanization and the growing impacts of climate change. She also investigates questions on urban governance and rural-urban transitions in cities of the global South. At their core, all her projects interrogate how planning processes reflect and reinforce the status quo in moments of transition and how different social groups contest inequalities and transform planning at such moments to create just and sustainable futures.<\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c408"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c113","index":2,"id":"9-c116","partialId":9,"styleRef":1220,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c117","parentId":"9-c116","partialId":9,"styleRef":1221,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Website","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"https:\/\/www.geography.utoronto.ca\/people\/directories\/all-faculty\/nidhi-subramanyam"}},"domuuid":"9-c128"}],"domuuid":"9-c311"}],"styleRef":1217,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c172"}],"id":"9-c110","parentId":"9-c2","partialId":9,"styleRef":1214,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c169"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c119","parentId":"9-c118","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c119","index":0,"id":"9-c120","partialId":9,"styleRef":1216,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/LT.png","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1040,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c323"}],"styleRef":1215,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c121","parentId":"9-c118","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c121","index":0,"id":"9-c122","partialId":9,"styleRef":1218,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Laura Tozer

Dr. Laura Tozer is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Physical & Environmental Sciences at the University of Toronto Scarborough. Her research tries to understand how we can accelerate action to address the climate crisis. She studies the policies and politics that can help us stop using fossil fuels and transition to renewable energy. She\u2019s especially interested in understanding how governments and communities can rapidly change cities so that they are fairer, resilient to the impacts of climate change, and powered by renewable energy. She has conducted research on the planning and implementation of just, zero carbon and resilient transitions in cities; the politics of transnational urban climate governance; and pathways to mainstream sustainability solutions so that they become standard practice for urban Taneea is a Ph.D. student at the University of Toronto in the Department of Computer Science, with a specialisation in Environmental Studies. Her research focus is interdisciplinary and combines techniques of Human Computer Interaction in the application area of Climate Change. Her current research resembles social science informed computing and looks at the creation, use and communication of climate data practices, and climate modelling practices in the Greater Toronto Area. This work touches upon research areas in climate adaptation, civic technologies, data and data infrastructures and social justice.<\/span><\/p>

Rayan is a Computer Science, Bioinformatics and Statistics student at the University of Toronto, specializing in Human-Computer Interaction. Her research interests lie in climate change, migration, and the datafication and use of AI systems in socio-economic contexts. Rayan has a strong track record of championing equity initiatives at the University of Toronto. She founded and is of the Black STEM network and the Sudanese Student Union and serves at the Equity Director for the Black Students Association. Her advocacy extends beyond the campus. At the Toronto Youth Cabinet - the City of Toronto's official youth advocacy body - Rayan served as the Media Lead of the Urban Health Working Group. As a Youth Ambassador for the World Youth for Water and a Youth Ambassador for the International Red Cross\/Crescent societies, and numerous other non-profits and high-impact organizations, she advocates about the importance of leveraging emerging technologies to create a better future for people everywhere.<\/strong><\/p>

Mickell is pursuing a Ph.D. in Computer Science at the University of Toronto under the supervision of Prof. Steve Easterbrook. He has studied Meteorology and Environmental Science at the University of the West Indies and Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence at Liverpool John Moores University. Growing up in Barbados, Mickell's experiences with hurricanes and other meteorological phenomena sparked a deep interest in understanding and forecasting these systems. His research focuses on applying deep learning techniques to weather nowcasting and remote sensing, aiming to extend forecast times for hurricanes in the tropical Atlantic and enhancing meteorological satellite remote sensing capabilities in regions with limited ground-based observations.<\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c245"},{"name":"hop-link-group","parentId":"9-c147","index":2,"id":"9-c150","partialId":9,"styleRef":1272,"type":"content","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c151","parentId":"9-c150","partialId":9,"styleRef":1197,"type":"content","props":{"text":"LinkedIn","iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","link":{"value":"www.linkedin.com\/in\/mickell-als"}}}],"slot":null}],"styleRef":1193,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c408"}],"id":"9-c144","parentId":"9-c126","partialId":9,"styleRef":1190,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c279"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c153","parentId":"9-c152","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c153","index":0,"id":"9-c154","partialId":9,"styleRef":1192,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/03\/cropped-cropped-Arjav-e1680200085667.jpeg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":1355,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c168"}],"styleRef":1191,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c155","parentId":"9-c152","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c155","index":0,"id":"9-c156","partialId":9,"styleRef":1194,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Aarjav Chauhan

Harshit Gujral is pursuing a Ph.D. in Computer Science at the University of Toronto, where he studies how green technology can improve environmental and public health. A trained Data Scientist, Harshit uses methods from statistics and explainable machine learning to study how electric vehicles affect air quality and public health. His research aims to help policymakers in crafting environmental regulations that facilitate a rapid and equitable transition to green technologies. Harshit is also interested in studying the unintended rebound effects of technology, adopting a digital sufficiency approach to mitigate these effects in residential buildings, data centers, and machine learning infrastructures. As a doctoral fellow at the Climate Positive Energy and Data Science Institute, he contributes to pioneering research on sustainable energy solutions and data-driven environmental policy.<\/p>"},"domuuid":"9-c245"},{"name":"hop-link-group","children":[{"name":"hop-link","id":"9-c176","parentId":"9-c175","partialId":9,"styleRef":1197,"type":"content","props":{"iconName":"foundation-icons\/web","text":"Website","link":{"value":"http:\/\/iharshit.in\/"}}},{"name":"hop-link","parentId":"9-c175","id":"9-c177","partialId":9,"styleRef":1197,"type":"content","props":{"text":"LinkedIn","link":{"value":"https:\/\/www.linkedin.com\/in\/harshitgujral\/"},"iconName":"font-awesome\/linkedin-square"},"domuuid":"9-c429"}],"slot":null,"parentId":"9-c172","index":2,"id":"9-c175","partialId":9,"styleRef":1272,"type":"content"}],"styleRef":1193,"type":"content"}],"id":"9-c169","parentId":"9-c126","partialId":9,"styleRef":1190,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c279"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c179","parentId":"9-c178","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c179","index":0,"id":"9-c180","partialId":9,"styleRef":1318,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2024\/08\/cropped-IMG_4920-Navyata-Neeraj.jpg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":2055,"size":""}}],"styleRef":1316,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c181","parentId":"9-c178","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c181","index":0,"id":"9-c182","partialId":9,"styleRef":1194,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Navyata Neeraj"}},{"name":"hop-text","parentId":"9-c181","index":1,"id":"9-c183","partialId":9,"styleRef":1195,"type":"content","slot":null,"props":{"content":"

Allegra is a recent graduate from the University of Toronto with a Bachelors in Peace, Conflict, and Justice, and a specialization in environmental justice. Dr. Nadine Plachta is a Postdoctoral Fellow at the Department of Geography and Planning. Her work focuses on social and cultural transformations in contemporary Nepal and, in particular, the use of citizenship and belonging as a resource for governance and economic development. She has explored this theme in the context of infrastructural politics, land and natural resource conflicts, local ecological knowledge, and environmental management. Her most recent research explores how borderland communities reassess their expectations of the future within recurring situations of disaster and crisis. Her scholarship is based on long-term ethnographic engagement in South Asia, and, especially in Nepal where she lived and worked for Heidelberg University's South Asia Institute for five years (2014-2019). Nadine is also Editorial Team Member of the online journal Roadsides, as well as Book Reviews Editor of Himalayan, the Journal of the Association for Nepal and Himalayan Studies.<\/strong><\/p>"}}],"styleRef":1468,"type":"content"}],"id":"9-c245","parentId":"9-c229","partialId":9,"styleRef":1466,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c252","parentId":"9-c251","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c252","index":0,"id":"9-c253","partialId":9,"styleRef":1192,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2022\/11\/cropped-BownZhang.jpg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":823,"size":""},"domuuid":"9-c289"}],"styleRef":1395,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c170"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c254","parentId":"9-c251","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c254","index":0,"id":"9-c255","partialId":9,"styleRef":1398,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Bowen Zhang

Dr. Austin is a Postdoctoral Research Fellow at the University of Toronto, School of the Environment. He is an environmental anthropologist who studies issues related to disaster recovery and disaster risk management, water and energy, infrastructure development, climate change adaptation and climate science, and the politics of environmental data and knowledge production. His work focuses on the Himalayan bioregion, and primarily in Nepal. He holds a Ph.D. in Anthropology from Cornell University, an M.S. from the Yale School of the Environment, and a B.A. from Dartmouth.<\/strong><\/p>"}}],"styleRef":2030,"type":"content"}],"id":"9-c257","parentId":"9-c229","partialId":9,"styleRef":2028,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"25","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c264","parentId":"9-c263","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-image","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c264","index":0,"id":"9-c265","partialId":9,"styleRef":2039,"type":"content","props":{"url":"https:\/\/www.climateobservatory.ca\/wp-content\/uploads\/2023\/04\/cropped-cropped-Sophia-scaled-1.jpg","caption":{"text":""},"imageId":2052,"size":""}}],"styleRef":2037,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"75","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"9-c266","parentId":"9-c263","partialId":9,"children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c266","index":0,"id":"9-c267","partialId":9,"styleRef":2041,"type":"content","props":{"content":"SOPHIA JIT"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"9-c266","index":0,"id":"9-c268","partialId":9,"styleRef":2040,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

Prior to studying computer science at the University of Toronto, she completed her MA in Economics at the same institution and a BA with an honours degree in philosophy and major in Economics, at the University of British Columbia. Her research interests include severe weather risk communication and accessibility justice. Following the completion of her MSc degree, she is hoping to pursue doctoral studies in computer science.<\/strong><\/p>"}}],"styleRef":2038,"type":"content"}],"id":"9-c263","parentId":"9-c229","partialId":9,"styleRef":2036,"type":"content"}],"id":"9-c229","parentId":"9-c1","partialId":9,"styleRef":1390,"type":"content","domuuid":"9-c126"}],"id":"9-c1","partialId":9,"styleRef":387,"type":"content"}

{"name":"hop-content","children":[{"name":"hop-section","props":{"anchor":false,"name":"Initial Content","attrs":{"id":"initial-content"},"initialContentSection":true},"children":[{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":100,"unit":"%"}}}}},"children":[{"name":"hop-slider","children":[{"name":"hop-slider-item","children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"6-c6","index":0,"id":"6-c7","partialId":6,"styleRef":1953,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Who we are
"}},{"name":"hop-text","id":"6-c8","parentId":"6-c6","partialId":6,"styleRef":1954,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

\ud83c\udf0f The Toronto Climate Observatory (TCO) is an interdisciplinary research initiative housed at the University of Toronto that brings together diverse communities of inquiry and practice to support just, plural, and place-based climate action in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA). We are a growing network of researchers, students, practitioners, and community partners committed to transforming how we understand, respond to, and shape the future of a changing climate.<\/span><\/p>"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"6-c6","index":2,"id":"6-c9","partialId":6,"styleRef":1974,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

NEXT: OUR PHILOSOPHY ><\/span><\/p>"}}],"id":"6-c6","parentId":"6-c5","partialId":6,"styleRef":1952,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-slider-item","children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"6-c10","index":0,"id":"6-c11","partialId":6,"styleRef":1984,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Philosophy
"}},{"name":"hop-text","id":"6-c12","parentId":"6-c10","partialId":6,"styleRef":1985,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

\ud83d\udca1At the heart of our work is the belief that responding to climate change demands inclusive, grounded approaches that reflect the lived realities of diverse communities and local geographies. Climate change is global, but its impacts and drivers are deeply shaped by local contexts. <\/span><\/p>

In Toronto, these dynamics are tied to the legacies and ongoing processes of settler colonialism, resource extraction, industrialization, and urbanization in the Great Lakes region. The impacts of climate change that communities in Toronto face today are inseparable from these legacies \u2013 and these, together with the uneven social and ecological geographies of modern cities like Toronto, shape the unique vulnerabilities, lived experiences, and distribution of these impacts. Simultaneously, these impacts and experiences intersect with issues of housing affordability, food security, labour and migrant justice, Indigenous rights, and others, producing the specific conditions that characterize life and work in Toronto. It is at these intersections that our work investigates varied imaginaries of climate justice, equity-aware public infrastructures, and relational paradigms, in response to the conditions of climate change as they take place in and are enabled by the Toronto urban metropolis.<\/span><\/p>"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"6-c10","index":2,"id":"6-c13","partialId":6,"styleRef":1986,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

NEXT: MISSION ><\/span><\/p>"}}],"id":"6-c10","parentId":"6-c5","partialId":6,"styleRef":1983,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-slider-item","children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"6-c14","index":0,"id":"6-c15","partialId":6,"styleRef":1980,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Mission
"}},{"name":"hop-text","id":"6-c16","parentId":"6-c14","partialId":6,"styleRef":1981,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

 \ud83c\udfaf We conceptualize climate change as a deeply local, lived experience shaped by inequality, infrastructure, and history \u2013 which means that the data, tools, and methodologies that we leverage to build climate solutions must be grounded in the local contexts that characterise the GTA. <\/span><\/p>

However, as they stand today, traditional climate data, models, and planning tools remain disconnected from the lived realities faced by communities in the region \u2013 particularly those already marginalized by systems of environmental and social injustice \u2013 and fail to capture the full scope of local climate impacts such as housing precarity, energy insecurity, or mobility injustice.<\/span><\/p>

The TCO was founded to help address this disconnect: to develop new forms of climate knowledge and communication that are responsive to specific places, sensitive to diverse ways of knowing, and oriented toward collective action. Our mission is to identify and fill critical gaps in existing climate information and urban data infrastructures to support effective adaptation, equitable planning, and long-term resilience in the GTA and beyond.<\/span><\/p>"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"6-c14","index":2,"id":"6-c17","partialId":6,"styleRef":1982,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

NEXT: APPROACH ><\/span><\/p>"}}],"id":"6-c14","parentId":"6-c5","partialId":6,"styleRef":1979,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-slider-item","children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"6-c18","index":0,"id":"6-c19","partialId":6,"styleRef":1976,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Approach
"}},{"name":"hop-text","id":"6-c20","parentId":"6-c18","partialId":6,"styleRef":1977,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

 At TCO, we combine tools and insights from the natural sciences, social sciences, humanities, and human-centered design to create new ways of seeing and responding to climate change. Our approach is rooted in interdisciplinary collaboration and grounded in the specific needs of communities across the GTA.<\/span><\/p>

Our work eschews a conventional top-down approach, and instead prioritises a model of cooperative action research that encapsulates and investigates the systemic intersectional considerations of class, gender, race, and ethnicity that mould the experience of climate impacts for communities within Toronto. The GTA is not a monolith \u2013 and our work aims to unpack the myriad experiences of peoples and communities across different neighbourhoods and geographies.<\/span><\/p>

Whether it\u2019s flood data equity, urban heat informatics, equity in climate retrofits, or risk communication for vulnerable communities \u2013 we work across sectors and issues to identify the gaps between available climate data and the data communities, governments, and other local stakeholders actually need, and in which forms, for equitable resilience planning. Our research blends technical analysis and climate modeling with participatory and creative practices like oral history, citizen science, Indigenous scholarship, and art\/science collaboration. By integrating physical and social science approaches, we make climate knowledge more meaningful and usable at the local level, especially in contexts of rapid change and systemic inequity. Our work centers on the development of frameworks and infrastructure that prioritize knowledge co-production with communities, ethical data governance, and the co-design of tools for planning and adaptation.<\/span><\/p>"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"6-c18","index":2,"id":"6-c21","partialId":6,"styleRef":1978,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

NEXT: HOW WE COLLABORATE ><\/span><\/p>"}}],"id":"6-c18","parentId":"6-c5","partialId":6,"styleRef":1975,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-slider-item","children":[{"name":"hop-heading","slot":null,"parentId":"6-c22","index":0,"id":"6-c23","partialId":6,"styleRef":1965,"type":"content","props":{"content":"Collaboration
"}},{"name":"hop-text","id":"6-c24","parentId":"6-c22","partialId":6,"styleRef":1966,"type":"content","props":{"content":"

 <\/span>Though our primary focus is on the GTA, our work is informed by insights from other geographies, and we seek to bring those lessons home through shared research and learning. As climate change continues to reshape urban life, the need for local, equitable, and interdisciplinary climate action is urgent. Together, we aim to help meet that need by building new infrastructures and forms of knowledge that are more inclusive, place-based, and just.<\/span><\/p>

As we continue to grow, we invite collaboration with others working at the intersection of climate science, data, policy, community, and culture. Whether you are a researcher, a city official, a grassroots organizer, an artist, or a community member, we welcome your participation. Together, we can build new ways of seeing, sensing, and shaping climate futures \u2013 starting right here in Toronto.<\/span><\/p>"}},{"name":"hop-button-group","children":[{"name":"hop-button","id":"6-c26","parentId":"6-c25","partialId":6,"styleRef":1968,"type":"content","props":{"text":"Explore our <\/span><\/h3>

\ufeff<\/span>At TCO, we work to transform how climate data is produced, shared, and used in Toronto. Too often, traditional datasets overlook the lived realities of the communities most impacted by climate change, leaving critical gaps in our ability to plan and respond equitably. <\/span><\/p>

Our work addresses these gaps by assessing the availability, quality, and usability of climate information across the GTA and identifying where new forms of data are urgently needed. This means looking to the broader social and political dimensions of climate knowledge, particularly examining who collects data, who has access to it, whose experiences are represented, and which voices are excluded.<\/span><\/p>

It includes, for example, <\/span>producing new information<\/u><\/a> that spotlights the systemic architectures and incentives that facilitate disproportionate and outsized amounts of carbon emissions from particular sectors; <\/span>building data infrastructures<\/u><\/a> that ensure equity is central to flood resilience planning; or designing municipal frameworks that make monitoring and evaluation more transparent, participatory, and accountable. It means examining how forces like climate migration, displacement, and housing precarity are already reshaping the city, and what kinds of information are needed to prepare for these changes. Importantly, this work also strives to acknowledge colonial histories of exclusion in data and create space for Indigenous and community-led approaches, expanding what counts as climate knowledge and ensuring it can inform just and place-based adaptation.<\/span><\/p>

We approach this through human-centered and participatory design, combining technical analysis with community-informed perspectives. By doing so, we not only uncover where existing systems fall short but also co-create new infrastructures that prioritize transparency, accountability, and justice. Ultimately, reimagining climate data systems means moving beyond numbers alone to build knowledge frameworks that are responsive to Toronto\u2019s diverse communities, capable of directing resources where they are most needed, and aligned with a vision of equitable and place-based climate action.<\/span><\/p>","appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"}}],"id":"456-c38","parentId":"456-c37","partialId":456,"styleRef":2007,"type":"content"}],"parentId":"456-c2","index":1,"id":"456-c37","partialId":456,"styleRef":2006,"type":"content"}],"id":"456-c2","parentId":"456-c1","partialId":456,"styleRef":506,"type":"content"},{"name":"hop-section","props":{"anchor":false,"name":"Custom","attrs":{"id":"custom"}},"children":[{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"50","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"456-c43","parentId":"456-c42","partialId":456,"children":[{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"456-c43","index":0,"id":"456-c44","partialId":456,"styleRef":2002,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c33","props":{"content":"

\ufeff<\/strong>BUILDING JUST DATA INFRASTRUCTURES<\/strong>
<\/span><\/h3>


<\/p>","appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"456-c43","index":0,"id":"456-c45","partialId":456,"styleRef":2002,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c40","props":{"content":"

Bridging the technical and the social<\/em><\/strong><\/p>


<\/h3>


<\/p>","appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"}}],"styleRef":508,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c4"}],"id":"456-c42","parentId":"456-c41","partialId":456,"styleRef":507,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c3"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":74,"unit":"%"}}}}},"props":{"appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"},"children":[{"name":"hop-text","id":"456-c48","parentId":"456-c47","partialId":456,"styleRef":2008,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c39","props":{"content":"

Equitable climate action depends not only on the data we collect and information we produce, but also on the infrastructures that store, process, and make that data usable. At TCO, we work to strengthen the systems behind climate data in the GTA so that resources and investments flow to where they are most urgently needed. <\/span><\/p>

This means building infrastructures that are not only technically robust but also socially just \u2013 bridges between complex climate information and the communities, governments, and organizations who need it for action on the ground. Our work includes advancing platforms that provide <\/span>accessible, cloud-based tools<\/u><\/a> for analyzing large climate and satellite datasets, ensuring they meet the diverse needs of users rather than reinforcing technical or institutional silos.<\/span><\/p>

It also involves, for example, developing mechanisms to rapidly collect and share post-disaster data on the physical, social, and economic impacts in vulnerable communities \u2013 information that is often overlooked in traditional monitoring systems but essential for equitable recovery and resilience planning. By combining technical innovation with ethical governance and participatory design, we help create data infrastructures that are transparent, inclusive, and aligned with the principles of climate justice. In doing so, we hope to transform data systems from barriers into enablers of place-based adaptation across Toronto.<\/span><\/p>","appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"}}],"id":"456-c47","parentId":"456-c46","partialId":456,"styleRef":2007,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c38"}],"parentId":"456-c41","index":1,"id":"456-c46","partialId":456,"styleRef":2006,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c37"}],"id":"456-c41","parentId":"456-c1","partialId":456,"styleRef":2009,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c2"},{"name":"hop-section","props":{"anchor":false,"name":"Custom","attrs":{"id":"custom"}},"children":[{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"66.66","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"456-c51","parentId":"456-c50","partialId":456,"children":[{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"456-c51","index":0,"id":"456-c52","partialId":456,"styleRef":2002,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c44","props":{"content":"

\ufeff<\/strong>PUBLIC ENGAGEMENT, CO-CREATION, AND CITIZEN SCIENCE<\/strong>
<\/span><\/h3>


<\/p>","appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"456-c51","index":0,"id":"456-c53","partialId":456,"styleRef":2002,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c45","props":{"content":"

Making climate knowledge participatory<\/em><\/strong><\/p>


<\/h3>


<\/p>","appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"}}],"styleRef":508,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c4"}],"id":"456-c50","parentId":"456-c49","partialId":456,"styleRef":507,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c42"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":74,"unit":"%"}}}}},"props":{"appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"},"children":[{"name":"hop-text","id":"456-c56","parentId":"456-c55","partialId":456,"styleRef":2008,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c48","props":{"content":"

We believe that everyone \u2013 particularly communities on the frontlines of climate change \u2013 should be able to shape how climate information is produced and shared. Through community engagement, participatory platforms, and citizen science tools, our goal is to enable local stakeholders to co-produce critical climate knowledge, contribute data on local climate impacts, and participate in decision-making on how this data is presented, shared, and used. <\/span><\/p>

Our work aims to ground climate knowledge in place. This includes, for example, participatory mapping processes for heat vulnerability as uniquely shaped by the Toronto urban metropolis \u2013 a justice-based approach that moves beyond conventional heat maps and their quantitative bias, and instead emphasizes the social, cultural, and lived dimensions of vulnerability. Another example of this is our <\/span>Toronto Water Atlas<\/u><\/a> \u2013 a critical, collaborative re-imagining of communities\u2019 relationships with Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area\u2019s (GTHA) waterways.<\/span><\/p>

Our focus with this pillar is on participatory approaches that prioritize storytelling, community engagement and situated voices, local knowledge, relationship-building, and co-creation, centering the lived experiences of Toronto communities most impacted by varied climate risks. <\/span><\/p>

We also translate complex climate data into actionable insights for adaptation planning and work to democratize data access for local climate action. Through these efforts, we aim to redefine what counts as climate knowledge, decentralize how it is collected and used, and build community capacity for resilience on the ground.<\/span><\/p>","appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"}}],"id":"456-c55","parentId":"456-c54","partialId":456,"styleRef":2007,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c47"}],"parentId":"456-c49","index":1,"id":"456-c54","partialId":456,"styleRef":2006,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c46"}],"id":"456-c49","parentId":"456-c1","partialId":456,"styleRef":2010,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c41"},{"name":"hop-section","props":{"anchor":false,"name":"Custom","attrs":{"id":"custom"}},"children":[{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":"66.66","unit":"%"}}}}},"id":"456-c59","parentId":"456-c58","partialId":456,"children":[{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"456-c59","index":0,"id":"456-c60","partialId":456,"styleRef":2002,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c52","props":{"content":"

\ufeff<\/strong>COMMUNICATION, EDUCATION, AND COLLABORATION<\/strong>
<\/span><\/h3>


<\/p>","appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"}},{"name":"hop-text","slot":null,"parentId":"456-c59","index":0,"id":"456-c61","partialId":456,"styleRef":2002,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c53","props":{"content":"

Building networks for long-term impact<\/em><\/strong><\/p>


<\/h3>


<\/p>","appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"}}],"styleRef":508,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c4"}],"id":"456-c58","parentId":"456-c57","partialId":456,"styleRef":507,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c42"},{"name":"hop-row","children":[{"name":"hop-column","style":{"descendants":{"outer":{"columnWidth":{"type":"custom","custom":{"value":74,"unit":"%"}}}}},"props":{"appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"},"children":[{"name":"hop-text","id":"456-c64","parentId":"456-c63","partialId":456,"styleRef":2008,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c56","props":{"content":"

\ufeff<\/span>\ufeff<\/span>\ufeff<\/span>The TCO is a hub for learning, collaboration, and capacity-building. Our annual <\/span>Toronto Climate Summer School<\/u><\/a>,<\/u> <\/u>workshops, and conferences hold space for researchers, governments, students, and civil society to imagine the region\u2019s climate future together. Under the banner of the 2024 Beatrice and Arthur Minden Symposium on the Environment, for example, we brought together a diversity of engaged stakeholders \u2013 researchers, Indigenous representatives, government staff, students, and non-profits, amongst others \u2013 to host the <\/span>Ontario Climate Risk Workshop<\/u><\/a>. This two-day gathering provided space for stakeholders from across disciplines to develop shared, holistic understandings of climate risk and differential vulnerabilities across Ontario, and to co-develop shared agendas for research and action in addressing these risks and building climate resilience. <\/span><\/p>

We also focus on improving communications around climate data and information to democratize access. This includes making complex data meaningful for those who need them, such as through innovative, novel data visualizations that can make this information accessible and usable for local stakeholders to design responsive and equitable climate solutions. <\/span><\/p>","appearanceEffect":"fadeInUp"}}],"id":"456-c63","parentId":"456-c62","partialId":456,"styleRef":2007,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c47"}],"parentId":"456-c57","index":1,"id":"456-c62","partialId":456,"styleRef":2006,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c54"}],"id":"456-c57","parentId":"456-c1","partialId":456,"styleRef":2011,"type":"content","domuuid":"456-c49"}],"id":"456-c1","partialId":456,"styleRef":505,"type":"content"}
